newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.
newsitem.headline: Australian Broadcasting Corp Afternoon Update.

text.p: LOWEST INFLATION RATE FOR 25 YEARS
A big drop in mortgage interest rates has led to the lowest annual inflation rate since the tail-end of the recession in 1992.
The Bureau of Statistics figures show there was deflation in the three months to the end of June.

The consumer price index fell by 0.2 of a per cent in the June quarter, taking the annual inflation rate to 0.3 per cent. Falling mortgage repayments accounted for most of this, with charges dropping by 9.6 per cent during the latest three months, to be one quarter below what they were a year ago.

The underlying inflation rate, which does not include mortgage charges, and is used by the Reserve Bank when setting interest rates, has fallen to 0.7 per cent, the lowest level in at least 25 years, and below the Reserve Banks target range.
Economists say that with continuing high unemployment, and inflation under control, another cut in interest rates is likely, as long as tomorrow's wage figures show modest rises, as is expected.
Some analysts say a cut could come as early as Friday.
Meanwhile, Federal Treasurer, Peter Costello, said today's low inflation result, plus a growing economy and a Budget moving into surplus could be good for long-term jobs growth.
Mr Costello refused to speculate on another interest rate cut, but said the last cut, in May, was still flowing through.
He said the result means workers do not have to go out and look for a two or three per cent wage increase to keep up with prices.
"Prices are not moving any more in underlying terms than 1.7 per cent, and in headline terms, your dollar is actually buying more than it was", he said.
INDUSTRIAL RELATIONS COMMISSION PRESIDENT RESIGNS
The President of the Australian Industrial Relations Commission, Justice Deirdre O'Connor, has resigned.
The Federal Workplace Relations Minister, Peter Reith, says, during her tenure, the Commission has been subject to significant changes including the start of the Government's industrial reforms.
He has thanked her, saying her efforts as President have been untiring and professional.
He said on a personal level, he appreciated the good working relationship.
Mr Reith said the Government will make a decision about a replacment in due course.
PRESSURE FORCED SWISS BANKS TO PUBLISH ACCOUNTS: AUSTRALIAN JEWS

The Australia-Israel and Jewish Affairs Council says Swiss Banks are bowing to international pressure, by publishing a list of one thousand Jewish bank accounts frozen and hidden since the second world war.
Chairman Mark Leibler said the Swiss are responding because they have been accused of collaborating with the Nazis in hoarding gold which belonged to victims of the holocaust.
Mr Leibler said many Australian Jewish families will make claims for their relatives' accounts.
He said Swiss Banks have behaved dispicably.
"What's happening now is no different their responding, not to any newfound sense of morality, but I believe quite clearly to international pressures that have been brought to bear", he said.
$19 MLN FOR WEATHER-PREDICTING COMPUTER
The Bureau of Meteorology and CSIRO have paid $19 million for a super computer that will predict the weather up to seven days in advance.
By using the computer, the Bureau expects to be able to give five-day forecasts by the end of the year, and seven day forecasts within two years.
The CSIRO also plans to put the super computer to work on researching diseases and drugs, with extremely long simulations of molecular structures.
Managing director of NEC, which designed the super computer, Ben Okamoto, said the computer can perform 104 billion calculations per second.
NZ PM MAY DISCUSS BRIEFING PAPER FIASCO WITH HOWARD THIS WEEKEND
This weekend's Bledisloe match between the Wallabies and the All-Blacks may also see the country's two leaders going head to head.
New Zealand's Prime Minister Jim Bolger, has indicated he may raise the issue of the leaked South Pacific briefing papers when he meets John Howard for the game.
John Howard invitated his New Zealand counterpart to the match last month.
On radio in Wellington today Mr Bolger said while he was looking forward to the game, the meeting would also give him a chance to talk to John Howard about the papers.

Mr Bolger said although the papers made disparaging remarks about New Zealand's attitude to the Pacific Islands and also New Zealand, he said he thought Australia should mind its Ps and Qs. The New Zealand leader said he did not bellieve the document reflected John Howard's view.
AUSSIE RUGBY COACH SAYS WALLABIES CAN WIN BLEDISLOW MATCH
In Rugby Union, Australian coach Greg Smith believes the Wallabies can turn the tables on the New Zealand All-Blacks, and reverse the result of the defeat in Christchurch two weeks ago.
Smith was speaking in Melbourne, as the Wallabies prepared for a training session in the lead-up to Saturday's night match at the MCG.
The match will be the second in the best-of-three Bledisloe Cup series, and also Australia's first match in the Tri-Nation series which also involves South Africa.
Smith said there are some important lessons to learn from the 30-13 defeat in the first Cup match in Christchurch.
He said the Wallabies need to play the game with intensity from the beginning.
"It'll be a very, very intense test match and we just can't afford to give the All Blacks any start," he said.
